name: Hoi An food guide
summary: Hoi An’s bowl is cao lầu: thick rice noodles barely wet with pork broth, under char siu, crisp ram, and Trà Quế herbs, tossed while it is hot. Then a warm white rose dumpling, a bánh đập cracker with stir-fried clams in Cẩm Nam, and a cup of nước mót on the walk.
body: Eat cao lầu in the old town. People here call the noodles bánh, not mì: thick rice noodles with only a splash of pork broth, char siu, crisp ram, and herbs from Trà Quế. It looks like a cousin of mì Quảng, and it is a different dish.

White rose dumplings are one warm bite each: a thin wrapper, of rice flour or wheat flour depending on the cook, around shrimp and pork, topped with fried shallot and dipped in sweet-sour fish sauce. Cơm gà is the rice lunch, shredded chicken over yellow rice cooked in chicken broth and turmeric, with rau răm, a sour papaya salad or pickles, a bowl of soup, and ginger fish sauce or chili sauce.

Mornings start with bánh mì from a street stall. Cross to Cẩm Nam for bánh đập, the cracker you break by hand and eat with stir-fried clams. Hoành thánh comes fried or in broth, bánh xoài is the chewy sweet sold near the Japanese bridge, and nước mót is the herb drink you carry on the walk.
specialtiesLead: The dishes to know by name, and what each one tastes like.

sections.heading: More Hoi An dishes
paragraphs: Past the bowls above, Hoi An eats rolls you build at the stall, crackers, snails, porridge, and sweet soups. Bánh ú tro and bánh ít sit beside them on the market’s gift counters.

spots.name: Banh uot thit nuong
spots.note: Hot grilled meat rolled in soft wet rice paper with herbs, cucumber, star fruit, and green banana, then dipped. Some stalls grill pork on lemongrass skewers for a dip of soybean paste, peanuts, sesame, and chili; others roll grilled beef with a rich, mildly hot peanut sauce.

spots.name: Bun thit nuong
spots.note: Barbecued pork over rice noodles and salad greens, tossed in a sauce thicker than the northern bún chả dip. Some bowls add herbs, crisp chả ram, and sweet-sour fish sauce.

spots.name: Banh dap
spots.note: A crisp grilled rice-paper sheet clapped onto a soft steamed one, so it shatters when you press the middle. Dip it in anchovy sauce with a little sugar, fried-shallot oil or pineapple and lime, and chili.

spots.name: Hen xao
spots.note: Clams stir-fried with onion, scallion, and chili, finished with crushed roasted peanuts and eaten with crisp rice paper or bánh đập. The clams are sweet and salty against the heat of the chili.

spots.name: Hoanh thanh
spots.note: Hoi An’s wonton, filled with shrimp or with shrimp and pork, three ways: fried crisp under a tomato sauce, in a clear pork-bone broth, or on thin wheat noodles.

spots.name: Grilled pork rice-paper rolls
spots.note: Grilled pork still sputtering from the coals, rolled in thin rice paper with herbs, star fruit or sour pineapple, green banana, and a little bún. Dip it in fish sauce or mắm nêm.

spots.name: Tam huu
spots.note: A small vegetable-village roll: one land shrimp, a slice of boiled pork, and a sprig of mint, tied with a blanched scallion and dipped in sweet-sour fish sauce.

spots.name: Bun mam nem
spots.note: Soft rice noodles that soak up a rich fermented fish sauce with garlic, chili, and shrimp.

spots.name: Banh canh
spots.note: Thick noodles of rice flour or bột lọc under roasted pork, fish cake, seafood, and herbs, with green chili and garlic-chili fish sauce on the side.

spots.name: Chao ngheu
spots.note: Rice porridge with sea clams, ginger, scallion, and rau răm, eaten hot at the start of the day.

spots.name: Chao gao luc
spots.note: Brown rice cooked soft and eaten with braised fish, chili, and green dưa gang melon. A light bowl for the evening.

spots.name: Be thui
spots.note: Slices of grilled veal rolled in rice paper with herbs, anchovy mắm, and a green chili. Ride to Điện Bàn for bê thui Cầu Mống, charcoal-roasted young beef that eats slightly sweet, chewy, and nutty.

spots.name: Chan ga cay
spots.note: Soft chicken feet soaked in a hot sauce of chili, garlic, and onion. A street snack, not a meal.

spots.name: Oc xao bo toi
spots.note: Snails stir-fried with butter and garlic, with bánh mì on the side. An evening plate.

spots.name: Oc hap sa gung
spots.note: Snails steamed with lemongrass and ginger. An evening plate.

spots.name: Oc xao me
spots.note: Snails stir-fried with tamarind. An evening plate.

spots.name: Banh xoai
spots.note: A chewy glutinous-rice sweet, shaped like a mango seed and not made of mango. The filling is crushed peanuts and brown sugar, or peanut, sesame, and shredded ginger with a mild heat.

spots.name: Nuoc mot
spots.note: A lightly sweet herb drink, cold after a hot walk or hot in the wet months, usually carried away in the hand. The herbs vary by maker: monk fruit and licorice with ginger, lemongrass, cinnamon, lemon, green tea, and chamomile, or with chrysanthemum and lotus leaf.

spots.name: Che bap
spots.note: Soft, chewy Cẩm Nam corn in a sweet soup with rock sugar and rich coconut milk. The dish came from elsewhere; the corn is local.

spots.name: Che dau xanh
spots.note: Mung-bean sweet soup, fragrant with coconut milk.

spots.name: Che hat sen
spots.note: Lotus-seed sweet soup, fragrant with coconut milk.

spots.name: Xi ma
spots.note: Black-sesame sweet soup, also called chè mè đen: sweet, rich, and cool.

spots.name: Banh dau xanh
spots.note: A gift cake of mung bean cooked with pork, sweet, salty, and rich, dried until crisp and eaten with hot tea. A meatless cake is made too.

spots.name: Mam ca com
spots.note: Anchovy sauce salted from fish off Cửa Đại and Cù Lao Chàm, hot, and not too salty or too sweet. Spoon it on hot rice, or dip boiled hyacinth beans and garden greens.

sections.heading: Regional dishes
paragraphs: Mì Quảng is the Quảng Nam bowl, worth eating in town when the ride to Da Nang is another day: flat turmeric-yellow noodles in a shallow ladle of broth, with Trà Quế herbs, peanuts, and a rice cracker. Toss it rather than drink it. It is not cao lầu.

sections.heading: Casual dining
paragraphs: The old town is the meal. Chợ Hội An, the open market inside the heritage area, has a food hall for cao lầu and counters selling mắm cá cơm.
The night market runs along Nguyễn Hoàng, Công nữ Ngọc Hoa, Trần Quý Cáp, and Bạch Đằng, close to the old-town centre. Come after dark for the local bowls.

Tân Thành, the fishing village now inside Hoi An Tây, holds a market usually on Saturday and Sunday. Cross to Cẩm Nam for bánh đập and hến xào, walk Thái Phiên early for noodles and rolls, and look for bánh ướt stalls along the Hoài.

spots.name: Hoi An market
spots.note: The food hall for cao lầu, and the counters for mắm cá cơm. Go in the daytime.

spots.name: Hoi An night market
spots.address: Nguyễn Hoàng, Công nữ Ngọc Hoa, Trần Quý Cáp, and Bạch Đằng
spots.note: Evening stalls close to the old-town centre.

spots.name: Tan Thanh weekend market
spots.note: A fishing-village market, usually held on Saturday and Sunday. The days can move from week to week.

spots.name: Cam Nam
spots.note: The lane for bánh đập and hến xào, across the river south of the old town.

spots.name: Thai Phien
spots.note: Early-morning noodles and rolls.

sections.heading: Breakfast
paragraphs: Bánh mì is the baguette from an old-town street stall, the morning it is baked: a dense loaf with a crisp crust, still hot, with a slightly sweet crumb. Point at the fillings if there is a choice. Cháo nghêu is the other morning bowl, clams with ginger, scallion, and rau răm, and Thái Phiên is the early street for noodles and rolls.

seoTitle: Hoi An food guide — cao lầu, dumplings, and bánh đập
seoDescription: Toss cao lầu while it is hot. White rose is one warm bite. Bánh đập is the Cẩm Nam cracker over stir-fried clams, and nước mót is the herb drink for the walk.
